Network.Description: During setup the boot.net.anydesk.com domain is requested over TCP 443.

Direct peer-to-peer connections use TCP 7070 by default; the listening port is configurable and direct connections can be disabled. Successful or failed direct attempts may expose the peer address in endpoint network telemetry. The address may belong to a VPN or NAT gateway and does not identify the operator.

Relay-mediated sessions connect to AnyDesk servers over TCP 80, 443, or 6568. Network telemetry for the relay connection identifies the relay address; direct connections can separately expose the peer address.
AnyDesk server connectivity; at least one of the documented TCP ports must be accessible.

Disk.Description: Client configuration observed in the cited lab investigation. Contains the relay host (h=), port (p=) and RSA server key in the launch parameters; useful for recovering the configured destination offline, without proving a connection occurred.

Client UI configuration. The AccessShow* examples were observed set to false in abusive deployments, but their effect depends on client version; newer releases restrict hiding the banner and tray icon. Assess settings against the approved deployment and organization policy, not as proof of malicious activity.

ScreenConnect working directory, with version-specific subdirectories. The cited lab observed RunFile staging beneath <version>\Temp; Huntress observed execution directly beneath <version>. Legitimate administrators also deploy files here. Correlate file writes and execution with session logs and approved activity; the path alone proves neither human interaction nor malicious intent.

ScreenConnect installer filename reported in Huntress's September 2026 Power BI phishing investigation (published October 7). The Downloads path generalizes the reported download destination; the filename can also occur in legitimate deployments. Observed URL pattern was <tenant>.screenconnect.com/Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.exe?e=Access&y=Guest&t=<token>.

MSI staging path reported by Huntress in the September 2026 investigation. SCAutoFix.ps1 downloaded a second client from /Bin/ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi?e=Access&y=Guest and replaced the first client. This is a case-specific artifact, not a default installation path.

Direct-under-Users path generalized from C:\Users\ScreenConnect.ClientSetup (6).exe in Huntress's September 2026 investigation. The report mentions both this EXE name and the MSI staging path; neither is a universal ScreenConnect installer location.

EventLog.Description: Service installation observed as LocalSystem with automatic startup in the cited lab. The service image path included launch parameters for session type (e=Access), relay host (h=) and port (p=). Distinct client thumbprints can identify multiple installations; compare with the approved inventory.
Host user connected. In the cited lab, the message included the session label, relay URL and instance fingerprint. Use as corroboration; absence of these application events does not exclude activity.
Host user disconnected. Corroborates the end of that connection; it does not establish that all operator activity or spawned processes have stopped.
Files transferred, with the action stated, e.g. "Transferred files with action 'Run': ScreenConnect.ClientSetup (1).msi".

Network.Description: Cloud relay pattern observed in the cited investigations on TCP 443. The installer download hostname can differ from the relay hostname; collect both. This pattern alone does not establish trial status or malicious use.

Default self-hosted relay port (configurable). The h= launch parameter or service ImagePath may contain a custom domain or IP address, so a ScreenConnect domain list alone can miss these deployments. Compare the destination with approved infrastructure.

Registry.Description: Service ImagePath value can contain the relay host and port in client launch parameters. It can reveal a configured destination without network telemetry; the cited lab observed the registry write before DNS, but that event ordering is not guaranteed.

The cited case reported ScreenConnect.WindowsAuthenticationPackage.dll in the Authentication Packages value. Investigate that DLL entry against the approved deployment and loaded module provenance; this shared Windows registry location alone identifies neither ScreenConnect nor malicious activity.
Credential provider registration pointing to ScreenConnect.WindowsCredentialProvider.dll. Display name may be "SC FeedbackTool Credential Provider" in malicious deployments.
SafeBoot Network entry allowing ScreenConnect client to start in Safe Mode with Networking.
